text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 12:
Simple pulley used for lifting weights. In this the power must be equal to the weight to obtain equilibrium.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 12; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_012.html.

text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 13:
In this the lower pulley is movable. One end of the rope being fixed, the other must move twice as fast as the weight, and a corresponding gain of power is consequently effected.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 13; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_013.html.

text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 14:
Blocks and tackle. The power obtained by this contrivance is calculated as follows: Divide the weight by double the number of pulleys in the lower block; the quotient is the power required to balance the weight.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 14; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_014.html.

text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 129:
Chinese windlass. This embraces the same principles as the micrometer screw 111. The movement of the pulley in every revolution of the windlass is equal to half the difference between the larger and smaller circumferences of the windlass barrel.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 129; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_129.html.

text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 134:
Uniform circular motion into rectilinear by means of a rope or band, which is wound once or more times around the drum.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 134; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_134.html.

text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 389:
Lifting-jack operated by an eccentric, pawl, and ratchet. The upper pawl is a stop.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 389; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_389.html.

text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 494:
Tongs for lifting stones, etc. The pull on the shackle which connects the two links causes the latter so to act on the upper arms of the tongs as to make their points press themselves against or into the stone. The greater the weight the harder the tongs bite.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 494; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_494.html.
